root.note: Latin may have borrowed it from Etruscan; Wiktionary gives that only as a possibility.

history: Look at the hat on the ê of fenêtre: it marks the grave of a letter. Latin fenestra meant a window, an opening or a passage, and Old French wrote fenestre, already in the Couronnement de Louis around 1135. In the French of Paris, an s before another consonant stopped being pronounced, but the spelling kept it for a long time. In 1740 the Académie française officially brought in the circumflex instead. The same happened in tête (teste), hôpital (hospital) and forêt (forest). So here is a trick for English speakers: when you see ê, ô or â, try putting an s back. The verb défenestrer, ‘to throw out of a window’, was made later from the Latin, and it still has its s.
historyEinfach: Fenêtre comes from the Latin word fenestra. In old French it was written fenestre, with an s. Later people stopped saying this s. In 1740 the spelling changed: the s went, and the e got a little hat, ê. You find the same in tête and hôpital. Tip: put the s back, and you often find an English word: forêt, forest.

elsewhere.text: English borrowed many French words before the s fell silent, so it kept the s: forest, hospital. The French ê, ô or â often marks where that s was.
